headline: A hundred-mile push to Atlantis, and the eddy that made it worth the diesel
subhead: Yellowfin turned up on the east wall this week where the blue water finally pinwheeled in — the rest of the canyons stayed quiet.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, four hours out of Montauk, my mate leaned over the covering board and said the water looked like ink with a blue undertone — the kind of color you don't see enough of out here in August. We'd left the dock at 3:30, run the numbers to the east side of Atlantis, and by the time the sun cleared the horizon we had four lines in the water and no idea yet whether the color meant anything. By nine o'clock we knew. First fish came unglued at the leader — a yellowfin that shook a green machine on a short wind-on and left us staring at each other instead of at a fish in the box. Lost fish sting different offshore. You don't get a second cast forty miles from the beach. But we boated five more before noon, sixty to eighty pounds, clean fat fish that had clearly been eating well on whatever the eddy pushed in front of them.

That's the story of the week out here — an eddy of deep blue water pinwheeled in from the east and settled over the eastern and western sides of Atlantis, and the yellowfin followed it in like they were supposed to. We flagged this pattern building two weeks back and said the current behind it didn't look like it was breaking down anytime soon. It hasn't. If anything it's held tighter than I expected for mid-August, and that's the difference between a good trip and a burned tank of fuel with nothing to show for it.

The program that worked for us, and for a few other boats working that same water, was straightforward: green and rainbow colors trolled through the warmest, cleanest part of the water column from mid-morning into early afternoon, then a swap to black and purple in that gray light right at sunrise and again as the sun dropped. Ballyhoo behind the smaller lures, a naked or lightly-skirted bird spread out front to draw the eye, and cedar plugs mixed in the pattern for the smaller yellowfin that wanted something subtler than a full daisy chain. Depth wasn't the story this week so much as water color — find where that blue eddy water pinched up against the greener inshore stuff, usually somewhere around the temperature break on the east wall, and that's where the reels started going off. A couple mahi came through the pattern too, nothing big, schoolies mostly, but a welcome bonus when you're grinding a long troll line waiting on a bite.

I want to be straight about the rest of the trip, because I don't sell hope out here — I sell what I saw. We ran a leg over toward Veatch on the way home hoping to find a piece of that same water holding over structure, and it was dead. Clean, but dead. No bait showing on the sounder, no birds working, nothing. Hydrographer and Oceanographer, from what I've heard secondhand from a couple of boats that pushed that far east this week, were quiet as well — same story, no bait stacked up, no temperature break worth working. That eddy water hasn't spread that far east yet, and until it does, or until something else pushes bait onto those grounds, I wouldn't burn the extra hour and a half of running time to find out. Atlantis is where the fish are right now, plain and simple, and that's not a knock on the other canyons — it's just where the water decided to go this week.

Bigeye and bluefin didn't factor into our week at Atlantis, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. There's giant activity happening well to our west that everyone at the dock has been talking about, boats stacked five miles wide on fish, but that's not my water and I didn't see it myself, so I'll leave that report to the guys running it. White marlin showed nothing for us either — no shots, no sightings, nothing worth mentioning. Wahoo the same. This was a yellowfin week, full stop, and a solid one if you were in the right piece of blue water.

On the fuel math, since that's the real cost of doing business out here: Atlantis is roughly a hundred miles from Montauk, more like a hundred-twenty if you're running out of Block Island or the Rhode Island ports. Call it five hours at a sane cruise, less if you're willing to burn the extra fuel to push it. That's a ten-hour round trip before you ever wet a line, so you'd better have a reason to believe the water's there before you leave the dock — and this week, for the first time in a couple weeks, I did.

Looking ahead, the moon's building back toward the August 28th full, and tidal push should firm up over the next several days. If that blue eddy holds its position over Atlantis — and there's no sign yet that it's sliding off — I'd expect the yellowfin bite to hold too, maybe improve as bait continues to stack on that edge. If it starts drifting east toward Veatch or Hydrographer, that's the one thing that would get me to shift my run, and I'll be watching the water color closely on the way out next trip to see if it's moved. Until then, Atlantis is getting my fuel, and I'd suggest it gets yours too if you're making the run from Montauk, Block, or the Bay this week.
